lessonTitle: Career Planning: Development Plans, Skills Mapping and Reflection

blocks.text: You have finished a gearbox redesign project in which the bearing selection went well but you needed help with the tolerance stack-up. A graduate recruiter now asks, 'What do you want to be doing in three years, and what are you doing about it?' Engineers who can answer with evidence, not wishes, are the ones who progress towards professional registration.

blocks.markdown: Career planning is an engineering activity: it has a **requirement** (the role you want), a **current state** (what you can already do), a **gap**, and a **plan with measurable milestones**. This unit gives you three tools for the cycle: the personal development plan (PDP), a skills-to-role map, and a structured reflective model that turns experience into evidence of learning.

blocks.title: Personal development plan (PDP)
blocks.text: A written plan in which you set development goals, the actions that will achieve them, the resources needed, and dated success measures, and then review it at fixed intervals. A good goal is SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

rows: Get better at CAD
Complete the vendor's advanced surfacing course and model one assembly of 50 or more parts unaided
Course certificate; assembly reviewed by my supervisor
By end of month 4
Learn about project management
Shadow the project engineer on two stage-gate reviews and write a one-page summary of each
Two summaries signed off by the mentor
Within 6 months
Be more professional
Log at least 30 hours of structured CPD in the year, recorded with an outcome for each entry
Hours and outcomes in the CPD log
12-month review
blocks.caption: Turning vague aims into goals with a measure and a date.

blocks.markdown: Notice the pattern in the right-hand columns: each goal names an **observable output** (a certificate, a signed summary, a log) and a **date**. If you cannot say how you would show a goal was met, it is not yet measurable.

blocks.title: Rewriting a vague goal as a SMART goal
blocks.prompt: A graduate wants to 'improve at finite element analysis' before a mid-year appraisal in 6 months. Rewrite it as a SMART goal with a weekly effort figure, given the course needs 36 hours of study and practice, and she will work on it for 12 weeks only, taking 2 of those weeks as planned leave.

steps.text: Specific: choose the output. She will complete an introductory structural FEA course and analyse one bracket of her own design, including a mesh convergence check.
Measurable: the course certificate plus a one-page report on the bracket, reviewed by her supervisor.
Achievable: working weeks available are 12 minus 2.
Relevant and time-bound: the work supports her design role, and both outputs are due two weeks before the appraisal, leaving time to respond to review comments.

blocks.answer: SMART goal: complete the FEA course and a reviewed bracket analysis in 12 weeks, at 3.6 h per week over 10 working weeks.

blocks.markdown: To map your skills to a role, start from the **job description**, not from yourself. Split each requirement into the knowledge, skills and behaviours the employer will test, give each a **weight** reflecting its importance, then rate your own evidenced level (for example 0 to 5). Only count a rating if you can name evidence: a project, a report, a supervisor comment.

blocks.caption: Weighted coverage C of a role: w_i is the weight of requirement i, s_i your evidenced rating (0 to 5).

blocks.title: Mapping skills to a graduate design-engineer role
blocks.prompt: A job advertisement weights four requirements: engineering analysis 35%, CAD and drawing 25%, teamwork 20%, and manufacturing knowledge 20%. A candidate rates their evidenced skill as 2, 4, 3 and 5 respectively on a 0 to 5 scale. Find the weighted coverage and identify the priority gap.

steps.text: Weights as fractions sum to 1, so the denominator is 5 times 1.
Priority gap: the shortfall from 5, weighted by importance, is 0.35(5-2)=1.05 for analysis, against 0.25, 0.40 and 0 for the other three, so analysis is the largest gap and goes first in the PDP.

blocks.answer: Coverage is 66%; engineering analysis is the priority development area.

blocks.title: Gap = importance x shortfall
blocks.text: Rank development needs by importance multiplied by shortfall, not by shortfall alone. A large gap in a minor requirement may matter less than a small gap in a heavily weighted one.

blocks.markdown: Experience becomes learning only when you reflect on it deliberately. **Gibbs' reflective cycle** has six stages: *description* (what happened), *feelings* (what you thought and felt), *evaluation* (what was good and bad), *analysis* (why it went that way, using evidence or theory), *conclusion* (what else you could have done) and *action plan* (what you will do next time). Simpler models, such as Rolfe's 'What? So what? Now what?', compress the same loop into three questions.

rows: Description
What happened?
The prototype shaft failed the 2 h endurance run.
Feelings
What was I thinking and feeling?
I felt defensive because I had skipped a fatigue check.
Evaluation
What went well and badly?
Manufacture was on time; the stress analysis was static only.
Analysis
Why did it happen?
Keyway stress concentration is a known fatigue initiator.
Conclusion
What else could I have done?
Run a fatigue estimate and ask for a design review.
Action plan
What will I do next time?
Add a fatigue check to my design checklist before release.
blocks.caption: Gibbs' cycle applied to one project event.

blocks.title: Reflection is not description
blocks.text: Most weak reflective writing stops at the first two stages and recounts events. Credit comes from the analysis and action-plan stages, which must be specific and lead to a dated PDP entry.

items: Start from the target role and its requirements.
Weight each requirement and rate your evidenced level.
Rank gaps by weight times shortfall.
Write SMART goals for the top gaps with a date and a measure.
Review the plan at fixed intervals and reflect after each major project.

points: A PDP contains goals that are specific, measurable and dated, with actions and review points.
A skills map weights the requirements of a role, rates evidenced skills and ranks gaps by importance times shortfall.
Gibbs' cycle (description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan) turns a project experience into a concrete next action.

questions.stem: Which goal is best written as a SMART development goal?

options.text: Become more confident with materials selection
Pass the institution's materials selection short course with at least 70% by the end of March and apply it to one live project
Work harder on materials in the next few years

questions.correctOptionText: Pass the institution's materials selection short course with at least 70% by the end of March and apply it to one live project

distractorRationale.a: No observable output, measure or date, so it cannot be reviewed.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: it names the output, a threshold measure, a date and a relevant application.
distractorRationale.c: Vague effort and an open-ended timescale; nothing can be measured.
distractorRationale.d: Activity without a measure or deadline.

questions.explanation: A SMART goal needs an observable output, a measure and a deadline. Only the course with a pass mark and a date, applied to a real project, allows a reviewer to decide whether it was achieved.

questions.stem: A PDP goal requires 48 hours of study to complete a hydraulics short course. The plan runs from week 1 to week 14, but 4 weeks are unavailable because of a site placement. Assuming the hours are spread evenly over the available weeks, how many hours per week are needed? Give the answer in hours per week.
questions.explanation: Available weeks are 14 - 4 = 10. Hours per week are 48/10 = 4.8 h. Converting a goal into a weekly rate shows whether it is achievable alongside other commitments.

questions.stem: A job description for a maintenance reliability engineer lists vibration analysis as the most heavily weighted requirement. A candidate has a small shortfall in it and a large shortfall in a minor, low-weighted requirement. Which should be placed first in the PDP, and why?

options.text: The minor requirement, because the shortfall is larger
Vibration analysis, because importance times shortfall may still be larger than for the minor item
Neither; gaps should not be ranked

questions.correctOptionText: Vibration analysis, because importance times shortfall may still be larger than for the minor item

distractorRationale.a: Ignores weighting; shortfall alone is not the ranking criterion.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: gap priority is weight multiplied by shortfall, so a heavy weight can outrank a bigger shortfall in a minor item.
distractorRationale.c: Convenience may inform scheduling but is not the prioritisation basis.
distractorRationale.d: Ranking is exactly what makes a PDP focused.

questions.explanation: The lesson ranks needs by importance multiplied by shortfall. A small shortfall on a heavily weighted requirement can exceed a large shortfall on a minor one, so it is not safe to rank on shortfall alone.

questions.stem: A role weights four requirements: thermofluids 30%, controls 30%, project management 25% and communication 15%. A candidate's evidenced ratings out of 5 are 3, 4, 2 and 5 respectively. Calculate the weighted coverage of the role as a percentage.
questions.explanation: The weighted sum is 0.30(3)+0.30(4)+0.25(2)+0.15(5) = 0.90+1.20+0.50+0.75 = 3.35. Dividing by the maximum rating of 5 gives 0.67, so coverage is 67%.

questions.stem: After a pump commissioning, an engineer writes: 'The seal leaked because the shaft run-out exceeded the supplier's limit, a check I had not planned, and the datasheet shows leakage rises sharply above that limit.' Which stage of Gibbs' cycle does this sentence mainly represent?

distractorRationale.a: Description only says what happened, not why.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: it explains why the event happened using evidence (the datasheet).
distractorRationale.d: An action plan states what will be done next time.

questions.explanation: Analysis asks why the event occurred and supports the answer with evidence or theory. The sentence links the leak to a cause and cites the datasheet, so it is analysis rather than description or an action.

questions.stem: A reflective account that accurately recounts what happened and how the writer felt, but proposes no explanation or next steps, fully satisfies a structured reflective model such as Gibbs' cycle.
questions.explanation: Gibbs' cycle has six stages and the later ones, analysis, conclusion and action plan, carry the learning. An account that stops at description and feelings is incomplete and unlikely to lead to a PDP entry.

questions.stem: At the end of Gibbs' cycle you write: 'Next time I will complete a tolerance stack-up before releasing any drawing.' Where should this item go to make it most useful for your development?

options.text: Be filed with the project report and not revisited
Be added to the PDP as a dated, measurable action with a review point
Be deleted because it is obvious
Be shared only with the client

questions.correctOptionText: Be added to the PDP as a dated, measurable action with a review point

distractorRationale.b: Correct: the action plan feeds the PDP, closing the loop between reflection and development.
distractorRationale.c: Obvious lessons are still the ones people repeat; recording them is the point.
distractorRationale.d: The client has no role in your development plan.

questions.explanation: The final stage of the cycle is the action plan, and the PDP is where actions get a date, a measure and a review. Linking the two makes reflection produce measurable development rather than a one-off essay.

questions.stem: A second-year graduate engineer wants to become a project engineer within three years. Write three goals for a 12-month PDP, each with a measure and a timescale, and explain how you would review progress.
markingGuide: Three goals relevant to the project engineer role (for example planning/scheduling skills, budget awareness, stakeholder communication)
Each goal is specific with an observable output
Each goal has a measure of success (certificate, sign-off, log entry)
Each goal has a date or deadline within the 12 months
Goals are achievable alongside the day job (hours per week stated or implied)
A review mechanism such as quarterly meetings with a mentor or line manager, with the plan updated
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives goals that can be verified by someone else and that have dates. The review process (fixed intervals, a named reviewer, plan updates) is what makes the PDP a living document.

questions.stem: A candidate states on an application form that they are 'highly skilled' in CFD, but they have only used it once in a group project. Explain how to map this skill honestly to a role requiring CFD, and what evidence and next steps you would record.
markingGuide: Rate the skill using evidence, not self-perception (single group project suggests a low-to-moderate rating)
Identify concrete evidence: report, results, supervisor feedback, the candidate's own contribution to the project
Compare to the role requirement and its weighting to quantify the gap
Identify a development action to close the gap (course, supervised project, mentoring) with a date and a measure
Note that overstating skills is a professional-conduct issue as well as a hiring risk
questions.explanation: Skills mapping depends on evidenced levels compared with the requirement. Overstating a skill damages trust and leaves the real gap unaddressed, so the honest map leads to a better PDP.

questions.stem: During a team design-build project, a supplier delivered a gearbox casting two weeks late. The team missed its demonstration date, and you, as the procurement lead, had not set up a backup supplier. Use the six stages of Gibbs' cycle to outline a reflection, giving a specific, evidence-based analysis and action plan.
markingGuide: Description: factual account (supplier late by two weeks, demonstration missed) without judgement
Feelings: honest account of reactions (for example anxiety, defensiveness) and how they affected decisions
Evaluation: what went well (communication with team, partial demonstration) and badly (no backup supplier, no early chasing)
Analysis: causes with evidence, for example no risk register entry for single-source supplier, lead times not checked, using risk or procurement theory
Conclusion: alternatives that could have been taken (dual sourcing, earlier orders, buffer in schedule)
Action plan: specific, dated actions linked to the PDP (for example add supplier risk to the register and review lead times at each milestone)
questions.explanation: A full marking response covers all six stages and, in particular, supports the analysis with causes and evidence. The action plan must be specific and measurable so that it can be transferred to the PDP.
